cim_eredeti: The godfather of AI and Nobel Prize winner in physics warns: “If we don’t do that, we’re toast”
szoveg_eredeti:
Geoffrey Hinton, considered one of the godfathers of modern artificial intelligence, is increasingly concerned about the future of humanity. The British-Canadian scientist, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024 for his research on neural networks, believes we are approaching a point where machines will be smarter than their creators—a development that could leave us in an extremely vulnerable position.

“We should make them so they really care about us. And if we don’t do that, we’re toast.”

In an interview with The Telegraph during the Starmus festival, held in Tenerife, Hinton emphasized that the solution lies in ensuring that artificial intelligence genuinely cares about human beings, rather than relying on the assumption that we will always be able to keep it under our control.

“We should make them so they really care about us. And if we don’t do that, we’re toast,” warns the scientist, who has spent years warning about the potentially catastrophic consequences of a technology that he himself played a decisive role in developing.

His approach goes beyond simply recommending that we be polite to ChatGPT or thank our virtual assistants. Hinton believes that future artificial intelligence systems should be designed to make human well-being one of their core priorities. His fear is that we will end up creating entities capable of surpassing our intellectual abilities without necessarily sharing our interests.

One of Hinton’s most controversial claims is that he believes current artificial intelligences may already be conscious. The researcher argues that some models have proven capable of modifying their behavior when they detect that they are being evaluated—a capacity he interprets as a sign of consciousness.

“AI has just as much subjective experience as we do,” argues Hinton, who takes issue with those who categorically rule out this possibility without, in his view, offering a satisfactory definition of what it means to be conscious.

However, this interpretation is far from being a scientific consensus. Just on October 19, the journal ‘Nature’ published an article by researchers Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi in which they argue that intelligence and consciousness are distinct concepts. The authors believe that current AI systems lack some of the properties necessary to experience conscious states, no matter how convincing their responses may be.

The distinction is important because a machine capable of mimicking emotions or recognizing that it is being examined does not necessarily have to experience feelings. But regardless of how that debate is resolved, Hinton insists that the great challenge is not merely to develop increasingly capable artificial intelligences, but to ensure that those capabilities are developed without rendering their creators obsolete.
